Which could we model with **linear regression**?

##

Identify the response variable type:

- A car insurance company is trying to predict if an applicant will have a car crash in the next 5 years, based on their income.

. . .

Can we model using linear regression anyways?

##

Let's simulated data...

```{r}
#| echo: false
set.seed(359)

n <- 300

sim_crash_data <- data.frame(
  #has_child = rbinom(n = n, size = 1, prob = 0.4), 
  income = sample(25000:100000 / 1000, size = n, replace = TRUE) # Uniformly randomly samples
) |> 
  mutate(xb = -19 + 0.4 * income) |> 
  #mutate(xb2 = -19 - 2 * has_child + 0.4 * income) |> 
  mutate(pi =  1 / (1 + exp(-xb))) #|> 
  #mutate(has_child = ifelse(has_child == 1, yes = TRUE, no = FALSE))

sim_crash_data$car_crash <- sim_crash_data$pi |> 
  map_int(\(x) rbinom(n = 1, size = 1, prob = x))

```


```{r}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "50%"
ggplot(sim_crash_data, aes(x = income, y = car_crash)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Income (in $1000s)",
    y = "Car crash"
  )
```

##

What does it mean to fit a line to this data?

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "50%"
ggplot(sim_crash_data, aes(x = income, y = car_crash)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    x = "Income (in $1000s)",
    y = "Car crash"
  )
```

. . .

We don't get an error, but ...


## 

Linear regression assumes 
$$Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{1, i} + ... + \beta_p X_{p, i} + \epsilon_i \text{ and } \epsilon_i\sim N(0, \sigma^2)$$

so 

$$E[Y_i | X_{1, i}, ..., X_{p, i}] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{1, i} + ... + \beta_p X_{p, i}$$

. . .

What is the expectation of a binary variable?


##

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-width: 8

ggplot(sim_crash_data, aes(x = income, y = pi)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    x = "Income (in $1000s)",
    y = "Probability of car crash"
  )
```


## 

What is our expecation for people with an income of $45,000?

```{r}
crash_model <- lm(car_crash ~ income, data = sim_crash_data)

new_data <- data.frame(income = 45)

predict(crash_model, newdata = new_data)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-width: 8
pred_45000 <- predict(crash_model, newdata = new_data)

ggplot(sim_crash_data, aes(x = income, y = pi)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  geom_point(
    data = data.frame(income = new_data$income, pi = pred_45000),
    color = "red",
    size = 3
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Income (in $1000s)",
    y = "Probability of car crash"
  )
```

Invalid probability! 

##

We can fit a linear model for a binary response, but:

- the line is really fitting the $E[Y_i|X_i]$, the probability
- the range of $E[Y_i|X_i] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{1, i} + ... + \beta_p X_{p, i}$ is $(-\infty, \infty)$
- we may get invalid predictions

. . .

We can use a logistic model instead!

## Logistic function

The logistic function ranges from 0 to 1

$$\text{logistic}(Z) = \frac{e^Z}{1 + e^Z}$$

```{r}
#| echo: false
data.frame(Z = seq(-10, 10, by = 0.01)) |> 
  mutate(logistic_Z = exp(Z) / (1 + exp(Z))) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = Z, y = logistic_Z)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Z", y = "Logistic(Z)")
```


## Logistic regression: form 1

Let $Y_i | X_{1, i}, ..., X_{p, i} \sim Bernoulli(\pi_i)$, which means $E[Y_i | X_{1, i}, ..., X_{p, i}] = \pi_i$

The logistic regression model is
$$E[Y_i | X_{1, i}, ..., X_{p, i}] = \pi_i = \frac{e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{1, i} + ... + \beta_p X_{p, i}}}{1 + e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{1, i} + ... + \beta_p X_{p, i}}}$$

## Logistic Response Function Rewritten

$$\pi = \frac{1}{e^{-(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + ... + \beta_{p-1} X_{p-1})} + 1}$$

<!-- \begin{equation} -->
<!--   \begin{split} -->
<!--     \pi &= \frac{e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + ... + \beta_{p-1} X_{p-1}}}{1 + e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + ... + \beta_{p-1} X_{p-1}}}\\ -->
<!-- \pi + \pi e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + ... + \beta_{p-1} X_{p-1}} &= e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + ... + \beta_{p-1} X_{p-1}}\\ -->
<!-- \pi &= e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + ... + \beta_{p-1} X_{p-1}} - \pi e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + ... + \beta_{p-1} X_{p-1}}\\ -->
<!-- \pi &= e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + ... + \beta_{p-1} X_{p-1}} (1 - \pi)\\ -->
<!-- \frac{\pi}{1 - \pi} &= e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + ... + \beta_{p-1} X_{p-1}}\\ -->
<!-- \log(\frac{\pi}{1 - \pi}) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + ... + \beta_{p-1} X_{p-1} -->
<!--   \end{split} -->
<!-- \end{equation} -->


## Logistic regression: form 2

Through some algebra we can rewrite the model as
$$\log(\frac{\pi_i}{1 - \pi_i})  = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{1, i} + ... + \beta_p X_{p, i}$$

. . .

- Form 1 is useful for understanding why we use the logistic function
- Form 2 is useful for interpretation

## Logistic regression: form 2

$$\log(\frac{\pi_i}{1 - \pi_i})  = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{1, i} + ... + \beta_p X_{p, i}$$

- Left side is called the *log odds* or *logit*



## Probability and Odds

What are odds?
<!-- $$Odds = \frac{\text{Probability of success}}{\text{Probability of failure}} = \frac{P(Y = 1)}{P(Y = 0)} = \frac{P(Y=1)}{1 - P(Y=1)} $$ -->

\vspace*{1.5cm}

Relationship between probability and odds
<!-- $$\text{Probability} = \frac{\text{Odds}}{1 + \text{Odds}}$$ -->

\vspace*{1.5cm}


```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.75
#| echo: false

prob_seq <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.01)

prob_odds_df <- data.frame(
  "probability" = prob_seq,
  "odds" = prob_seq / (1 - prob_seq),
  "log_odds" = log(prob_seq / (1 - prob_seq))
)

gridExtra::grid.arrange(
  ggplot(prob_odds_df, aes(x = probability, y = odds)) +
    geom_point() +
    labs(x = "Probability", y = "Odds") +
    theme_bw(base_size = 20),
  ggplot(prob_odds_df, aes(x = probability, y = log_odds)) +
    geom_point() +
    labs(x = "Probability", y = "Log Odds") +
    theme_bw(base_size = 20),
  nrow = 1
)
```

## Parameter Interpretation: Solving for $\beta_1$

$$\log(\frac{\pi}{1 - \pi}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + ... + \beta_{p-1} X_{p-1}$$
Now we have a model that connects $E[Y|X] = \pi$ to our data, but how do we interpret the parameters, $\beta_j$'s?

Recall for linear regression: $E[Y|X] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X$

<!-- \begin{equation*} -->
<!--   \begin{split} -->
<!--     &\color{blue}{E[Y|X=x+1]} - \color{purple}{E[Y|X=x]}\\ -->
<!--     &=\color{blue}{\beta_0 + \beta_1(x + 1)} - (\color{purple}{\beta_0 + \beta_1x})\\ -->
<!--     &=\color{blue}{\beta_0} + \color{blue}{\beta_1x} + \color{blue}{\beta_1} - \color{purple}{\beta_0} - \color{purple}{\beta_1x}\\ -->
<!--     & = \beta_1 -->
<!--   \end{split} -->
<!-- \end{equation*} -->
<!-- So -->
<!-- $\beta_1$ = change in expected value of Y associated with a 1 unit change in X. -->

## Parameter Interpretation: Solving for $\beta_1$

$$\log(\frac{E[Y|X]}{1 - E[Y|X]}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X$$

<!-- \begin{equation*} -->
<!--   \begin{split} -->
<!--     &\color{blue}{\log(\frac{E[Y|X = x + 1]}{1 - E[Y|X = x + 1]})} - \color{purple}{\log(\frac{E[Y|X = x]}{1 - E[Y|X = x]})}\\ -->
<!--     &= \color{blue}{\beta_0 + \beta_1 (x + 1)} - (\color{purple}{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x)}\\ -->
<!--     &= \color{blue}{\beta_0} + \color{blue}{\beta_1 x} + \color{blue}{\beta_1} - \color{purple}{\beta_0} - \color{purple}{\beta_1 x}\\ -->
<!--     &= \beta_1 -->
<!--   \end{split} -->
<!-- \end{equation*} -->

<!-- Let $\color{blue}{\pi_a = E[Y | X = x + 1]}$ and $\color{purple}{\pi_b = E[Y | X = x]}$, -->

<!-- \begin{equation*} -->
<!--   \begin{split} -->
<!--     \color{blue}{\log(\frac{\pi_a}{1 - \pi_a})} - \color{purple}{\log(\frac{\pi_b}{1 - \pi_b})} &= \beta_1\\ -->
<!--     \log(\color{blue}{\frac{\pi_a}{1 - \pi_a}} / \color{purple}{\frac{\pi_a}{1 - \pi_a}}) & = \beta_1 -->
<!--   \end{split} -->
<!-- \end{equation*} -->

## Parameter Interpretation: Explaining $\beta_1$

Odds Ratio

$e^{\beta_1} = \frac{\pi_a}{1-\pi_a} / \frac{\pi_b}{1-\pi_b}$

\vspace*{1.25cm}

If $e^{\beta_1}$ = 1

\vspace*{1cm}

If $e^{\beta_1}$ < 1

\vspace*{1cm}

If $e^{\beta_1}$ > 1


## Parameter Estimation: Maximum Likelihood Estimate

We want the Maximum Likelihood Estimate (MLE) for the $\beta_j$'s... why?

The MLE aims to find estimates $\hat{\theta} = \{\hat{\beta}_0, \hat{\beta}_1, ..., \hat{\beta}_{p-1}\}$ that maximize the likelihood function over the parameter space with a given data set.

\vspace*{0.75cm}

The likelihood function measures the goodness of fit of a statistical model to a sample of data for given values of the unknown parameters $\theta$.
$$L(\theta | y) = f_{\theta}(y) = Pr(y | \theta)$$

\vspace*{0.75cm}

We want to find $\hat{\theta}$ to maximize $L(\theta | y)$

## Parametr Estimation: MLE for Logistic Regression

$$Y_i | X = x_i \sim Bernoulli(\pi_i),$$
Where
$$\pi_i = \frac{e^{\beta_1 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + ... + \beta_{p-1} x_{(p-1)i}}}{1 + e^{\beta_1 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + ... + \beta_{p-1} x_{(p-1)i}}}.$$

We want to maximize

$L(\theta | y)$


## Parameter Estimation: MLE for Linear Regression

Why didn't we do this for linear regression?
...

We did! But Ordinary Least Square estimates for the $\beta_j$'s in linear regression happen to be the MLE

- OLS is easier to solve than MLE for linear regression, so we choose to introduce it with OLS instead of solving for the $\hat{\theta} = (\hat{\mu}_i, \hat{\sigma}^2)$ that maximize
$$L(\theta | y_i) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^2}} \exp\{-\frac{(y_i - \mu_i)}{2\sigma^2}\},$$
with $\mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + ... + \beta_{p-1} x_{(p-1)i}$

## Inference With Logistic Regression

In linear regression we used a t-test to test for statistically significant features.

Beware in logistic regression there are different tests that can be used

Likelihood Ratio Test

\vspace*{1.5cm}

Wald Test

\vspace*{2cm}

Know which one your software is using!

## Confusion Matrix: Sensitivity

1.) Sensitivity (= Recall, True Positive Rate)

\vspace*{0.75cm}

- TP + FN = # of actual ____________
- How well does the model classify/predict the positive value among the actual positive samples?
- How well does the model detect positive samples accurately?
- Example: Detecting spam emails
    - What percentage of spam emails does the model detect among the actual spam emails?
    
:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
  ![](confusion-matrix.png){width=2in fig-align="right"}
:::

::::
    
## Confusion Matrix: Specificity 

2.) Specificity (= Selectivity, True Negative Rate)

\vspace*{0.75cm}

- TN + FP = # of actual _______________
- How well does the model classify/predict the negative value among the actual negative samples?
- How well does the model eliminate negative samples accurately?
- Example: Detecting spam emails
    - What percentage of non-spam emails does the model detect among the actual non-spam emails?
    
:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
  ![](confusion-matrix.png){width=2in fig-align="right"}
:::

::::

## Confusion Matrix: Trade-off

3.) Trade-off between sensitivity and specificity

- How to make our model detect all the actual positives?

\vspace*{1cm}

4.) Best model = high sensitivity \& high specificity $\rightarrow$ F1-score
